desc:
A hiker may pack at most k of n distinct items, and the total weight must not exceed capacity. Item i weighs weights[i] and is worth values[i]; each item can be taken at most once.

Return the largest total value the hiker can pack. Taking nothing is allowed, so the answer is never negative.

weights = [3, 4, 2, 5], values = [40, 50, 30, 70], k = 2, capacity = 8 -> 110   (items 0 and 3)
weights = [3, 4, 2, 5], values = [40, 50, 30, 70], k = 3, capacity = 9 -> 120   (items 0, 1, 2)
weights = [3, 4, 2, 5], values = [40, 50, 30, 70], k = 1, capacity = 9 -> 70
hints: A plain knapsack table has one dimension (weight). The extra limit on the number of items asks for a second dimension.
Let best[j][c] be the largest value using at most j items of total weight at most c, over the items processed so far.

For each item (weight w, value v), update best[j][c] = max(best[j][c], best[j-1][c-w] + v) with j going from k down to 1 (and c downward as well, or by using the old row), so every item is used once. Answer: best[k][capacity].
editorial: Add a second axis to the knapsack: the number of items used. Define best[j][c] as the maximum value obtainable from the items seen so far using at most j of them with total weight at most c. Starting with all zeros already encodes the empty choice, and because both limits are "at most", the table is monotone in j and c.

Processing an item with weight w and value v creates the candidate best[j-1][c-w] + v for every j ≥ 1 and c ≥ w. The candidate reads a row with one fewer item that must still describe the state before this item, so the rows are visited from j = k downward (and within a row c is read from the previous row, never from itself). The cost is O(n · k · capacity) time and O(k · capacity) space. The same pattern handles any problem with two independent limits, such as a weight limit and an item-count limit.
